newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Norway's Brundtland tells U.S. to pay up.
newsitem.headline: Norway's Brundtland tells U.S. to pay up.

text.p: Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland, often mentioned as a candidate for U.N. secretary-general, indirectly hit the United States on Monday for not paying dues but throwing its weight around.
In her speech to the U.N. General Assembly, she called for major reforms, saying that "an organisation that fails to change is bound to lose its effectiveness."
"But we cannot accept intimidation. Withholding legally assessed contributions amounts to just that," she said in an obvious reference to the United States.

Washington owes $1.6 billion, more than half of the $2.9 billion United Nations debt. Congress had made various reform measures a condition for paying part of the debt and has unilaterally imposed a cap on U.S. contributions.

The Clinton administration has also vowed to block another five-year term for Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali this year but has not proposed a candidate of its own. Brundtland did not touch on the election controversy.

Brundtland, a leading world expert on environment, also announced a Fund for Preventive Action that Norway would launch with several million dollars a year so the United Nations could react diplomatically to crises quickly.

"We know that the hands of the secretary-general often are tied in such cases when it comes to redirecting resources. U.N. expertise -- our expertise -- may not show up because there is not sufficient funds for air tickets," she said.
On reform of the world body, she said the world needed a leaner and stronger structure and less duplication of efforts on the country level.
"We are not served by protracted denials of the world as it is," she said.
"Today there are several U.N. representatives in one country, often overlapping each other and often contributing to more fragmentation," she said.
Brundtland also called on the United Nations to talk more about human rights, saying that in a world of global communication the facts could no longer be hidden.

"We cannot build fences around ideas in the age of Internet," she said. "It will be increasingly impossible to derive the benefits of the global economy without exposing political power structure to the scrutiny of democracy."
